title.text: Neural networks and deep learning, without the maths wall

objects.text: What is a neural network, and when is one the right tool?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 20 of 24  |  Module E: Neural networks and text
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Neural networks have a reputation for being magic, or for needing a wall of mathematics. Today we remove both. A neuron is a weighted sum with a bend. A network is many of them. Training is a loop of small corrections that you will run yourself in numpy.

And then the practical question: for a table like our loans, is a network worth it, or does a simpler model do the job? You will find out with your own numbers.

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can describe an artificial neuron, the layers of a network, the loss function and gradient descent, using the real terms and a plain explanation of each. You can run a neuron and a real gradient descent loop in numpy, and you can watch a network overfit.

And you can compare an MLPClassifier with a random forest on the loans data, and say when deep learning is worth the trouble. There is very little algebra today. Everything is numbers you can check.

title.text:
Your two hours: network ideas
first, then the neural network lab

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x2.95_bd087db9.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Ideas with pictures first. Then you open the notebook and TensorFlow Playground.

slides.notes:
We have two hours. The first ten minutes bring back Session 19 and set the question. Then forty-five minutes of concepts with laptops closed: the neuron, the layers, the loss, gradient descent, overfitting, and pretrained models. After a ten minute break you open the notebook for a forty-five minute lab.

You build a neuron and a training loop in numpy, play with TensorFlow Playground, and compare a network with a random forest on the loans. The last ten minutes are the exit check and what you keep.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  Why do we split a time series by date?
2.  What must a forecast beat before you trust it?
3.  Why do we group by district before we shift a lag feature?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 19. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Why do we split a time series by date?

A good answer is this. A random split lets the model see months after the test months, which is data leakage. Next month always lies after the data you have.

Question two. What must a forecast beat before you trust it?

A good answer is this. The baseline model: the seasonal naive forecast that copies the same month from last year.

Question three. Why do we group by district before we shift a lag feature?

A good answer is this. Without groupby, the first month of a district borrows its lag from the district above it in the file.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 19

rows.text: Why do we split a time series by date?
A random split lets the model see months after the test months, which is data leakage. Next month always lies after the data you have.
What must a forecast beat before you trust it?
The baseline model: the seasonal naive forecast that copies the same month from last year.
Why do we group by district before we shift a lag feature?
Without groupby, the first month of a district borrows its lag from the district above it in the file.

Here are the answers to the three warm-up questions. We split a time series by date because a random split would let the model see months after the test months. That is data leakage, and next month always lies after the data you have. A forecast must beat the baseline model, the seasonal naive forecast that copies the same month from last year.

And we group by district before we shift, because otherwise the first month of a district borrows its lag from the district above it. Today the same test applies to a neural network: it must beat a simple model. Which of the three did you find hardest?

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A small calculation: a weighted sum of the inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function.
The bend applied to the weighted sum. Sigmoid gives a score from 0 to 1. ReLU gives 0 below zero and the total above it.
Neurons arranged in an input layer, hidden layers and an output layer, with values moving forward only.
Training: repeated small steps that lower the loss function. Backpropagation works out how much each weight changed the loss (its gradient).
Start from a network someone else trained and train only a new last layer on your own data.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Artificial neuron (perceptron). A small calculation: a weighted sum of the inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function.

Activation function (sigmoid, ReLU). The bend applied to the weighted sum. Sigmoid gives a score from 0 to 1. ReLU gives 0 below zero and the total above it.

Feedforward neural network (multilayer perceptron, MLP). Neurons arranged in an input layer, hidden layers and an output layer, with values moving forward only.

Gradient descent and backpropagation. Training: repeated small steps that lower the loss function. Backpropagation works out how much each weight changed the loss (its gradient).

Transfer learning (pretrained model). Start from a network someone else trained and train only a new last layer on your own data.

title.text:
An artificial neuron is a weighted sum plus a
bias, passed through an activation function

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsj_neuron_11.90x4.25_c8deee8c.png
objects.alt: An artificial neuron is a weighted sum plus a bias, passed through an activation function

objects.text: Illustrative loan and weights, never trained. Spreadsheet word for the sum: SUMPRODUCT.

slides.notes:
The smallest piece of a neural network is one artificial neuron, also called a perceptron. Here it scores one loan. The inputs are two late payments, savings of 0.4 million shillings, and a loan of 0.6 million. These weights are made up, to show the arithmetic. Each input is multiplied by its weight, and the three results are added with a bias of minus one.

That gives a weighted sum, z, of 1.22. Then the activation function, here a sigmoid, bends z into a score between 0 and 1. The score is 0.772. In a spreadsheet the weighted sum is SUMPRODUCT. Which input pushes the risk up, and which pushes it down?

slides.notes:
Every part of a neuron has an Excel cousin. The weighted sum is SUMPRODUCT. The weights are the multipliers beside each input, and they are the parameters that training adjusts. The bias is the constant added at the end, the intercept you know from regression. The activation function is like an IF or a MAX wrapped round a formula.

A hidden layer is a set of helper columns between the data and the answer. And the loss function is the total of an error column. Careful with the word bias. Here it is the intercept, which is a different idea from the bias in the bias-variance trade-off.

Which of these rows is new to you?

title.text:
The neuron as formulas: z is the weighted
sum plus bias, and a is the activation

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.86_34c52baf.png
objects.alt: The neuron as formulas: z is the weighted sum plus bias, and a is the activation

rows.text: An input: one variable of the loan.
A weight: how much that input counts.
The weighted sum plus the bias.
The sigmoid: squashes z into 0 to 1.

objects.text: This is the logistic regression you met in Session 15, packaged as one unit.

slides.notes:
Here is the same neuron as formulas. The weighted sum plus bias, z, is w one times x one, plus w two times x two, plus w three times x three, plus b. The sigmoid of z is one divided by one plus e to the power of minus z.

With our numbers, z is 1.22, and the sigmoid of 1.22 is 0.772. Notice that this is exactly the logistic regression you met in Session 15. A neuron with a sigmoid is a logistic regression packaged as one unit. A network is many of these stacked. Which symbol on the table would training change?

title.text:
Activation functions bend the total: sigmoid gives
a probability and ReLU is common in hidden layers

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsj_activations_11.90x4.25_5bdcdd6b.png
objects.alt: Activation functions bend the total: sigmoid gives a probability and ReLU is common in hidden layers

objects.text: ReLU (rectified linear unit): 0 for a negative total, the total itself otherwise.

slides.notes:
The bend has a proper name, the activation function. On the left, the sigmoid squashes any total into a score between 0 and 1, which makes it right for a probability. On the right, ReLU, the rectified linear unit, gives 0 for a negative total and passes a positive total straight through.

The gold dot is our neuron: z of 1.22 gives 0.772 on the sigmoid, and 1.22 on ReLU. Why bend at all?

Without a bend, stacking neurons would still give a straight line, however many you stack. The bend is what lets a network learn curves. Which of the two would you put in the output of a default model?

title.text:
Layers stack neurons into a feedforward
neural network (multilayer perceptron, MLP)

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsj_mlp_11.90x4.25_43ed5500.png
objects.alt: Layers stack neurons into a feedforward neural network (multilayer perceptron, MLP)

objects.text: Our loans network: 12 variables in, 16 and 8 neurons, 1 probability out. 353 weights and biases.

slides.notes:
Put neurons side by side and you have a layer. Feed one layer into the next and you have a feedforward neural network, also called a multilayer perceptron, or MLP. On the left, the input layer has one node for each of the twelve variables of a loan, the same twelve as Session 17.

Then two hidden layers, with sixteen and eight neurons. They are hidden because you never see their values in your data. The last circle is the output layer, one sigmoid neuron that gives the chance of default. Every line carries a weight, and every neuron has a bias.

Count them all and the network has 353 parameters. Why is it called feedforward?

title.text:
Reading the network: layers, parameters
and the arithmetic behind the count

rows.text: One node per variable. It holds the data.
Neurons that build new variables from the old ones.
Every weight and bias that training adjusts.
Values move from input to output, never backwards.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_grid_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_gear_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.34.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_key_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_flag_0.50.png

objects.text: More neurons mean more parameters, and more room to memorise the training set.

slides.notes:
Here are the terms again, with the loans network. The input layer holds the data, twelve variables. The hidden layers build new variables from the old ones, sixteen neurons and then eight. The output layer is the prediction. The parameters are every weight and bias. Between the inputs and the first hidden layer there are twelve times sixteen weights plus sixteen biases, which is 208.

Then sixteen times eight plus eight, which is 136. Then eight times one plus one, which is 9. Together, 353. Logistic regression on the same data has only 13. Why might more parameters be a risk?

title.text:
The loss function is one number
for how wrong the predictions are

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.80_29ebf9dd.png
objects.alt: The loss function is one number for how wrong the predictions are

objects.text: A classifier usually uses log loss (cross-entropy). Training means lowering the loss.

slides.notes:
To train a network we need one number that says how wrong it is. That is the loss function. For one record, the squared error loss is the prediction minus the actual value, squared. Here is a tiny example you will run yourself. One input, x equals two, and the target is six.

The prediction is two times the weight w, so the loss is two w minus six, squared. At w equal to zero, the loss is thirty-six. A classifier usually uses log loss instead, also called cross-entropy, but the idea is the same: training means lowering the loss. What weight gives a loss of zero?

title.text:
Gradient descent walks the weight
downhill: w goes from 0 to 2.95 in 8 steps

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsj_descent_7.70x4.80_b9f7e82d.png
objects.alt: Gradient descent walks the weight downhill: w goes from 0 to 2.95 in 8 steps

objects.text: Gradient descent lowers the loss one small step at a time.

runs.text: Gradient: the slope of the loss at the current weight.
Learning rate: the size of each step.
New weight = old weight minus learning rate times gradient.

slides.notes:
This is the loss curve for our one-weight example. The horizontal axis is the weight, the vertical axis is the loss. We start at w equal to zero, where the loss is thirty-six. At each step we measure the gradient, which is the slope of the curve at that point, and we move the weight a little downhill.

The size of the move is the learning rate times the gradient. Look at the dots: the first steps are big because the slope is steep, and the steps shrink as we near the bottom. After eight steps the weight is 2.95, close to the best value of 3.

Why do the steps shrink by themselves?

title.text: Read the recipe: gradient descent on one weight

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Line 1 sets the input, target, start weight and learning rate.
Line 3 is the loss. Line 4 is the gradient.
Line 5 moves the weight against the slope.
Real output: w climbs to 2.95, the loss falls toward 0.

slides.notes:
Read this recipe. Line one sets the input, the target, the starting weight and the learning rate. The loop runs eight steps. Each step computes the loss, then the gradient, which is two times the error times the input, then moves the weight against the slope. The output is real, and it prints steps one, two, four and eight.

The weight goes from zero to 1.2 on the first step, then 1.92, then 2.611, and ends at 2.95. The loss printed on each line is the loss before that step, so it falls from thirty-six toward zero. A real network does exactly this, with thousands of weights instead of one.

In the lab you run this loop yourself. What would happen if the learning rate were bigger?

title.text:
The learning rate decides whether
training settles, bounces or blows up

rows.text: Settles: each step is smaller than the last.
Bounces: the weight jumps between 0 and 6 and never settles.
Blows up: each step overshoots by more than the last.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.50.png

objects.text: Same loop, same target. Best weight: 3, loss 0. The recipe on the last slide prints the loss before each update, so its last line shows a larger loss.

slides.notes:
The learning rate is the size of each step, and it matters a great deal. With 0.05, the weight settles near 3 and the loss after the eighth update is 0.010. The recipe prints the loss before each update, so its last line shows a larger number. With 0.25, every step overshoots exactly to the other side, so the weight jumps between 0 and 6 forever and the loss stays at 36.

With 0.5, each step overshoots by more than the last, and after eight steps the weight is minus 19,680 and the loss is about 1,549,681,956. In real networks you see this as a loss that stops falling or turns into a not-a-number error. What would you try first if the loss rose?

title.text:
Backpropagation works out how much each weight
changed the loss, so gradient descent can adjust them all

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_network_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Backpropagation works out how much each weight changed the loss, so gradient descent can adjust them all

objects.text: Backpropagation: send the error backwards to find each weight's gradient, its effect on the loss.

slides.notes:
With one weight, the gradient is easy. A network has thousands. Backpropagation is the method that finds the gradient of every weight. First the network makes a forward pass: the inputs go through the layers and produce a prediction. Then we compute the loss. Then the error flows backward, from the output layer toward the inputs, and for each weight we work out how much it changed the loss, which is its gradient, using the chain rule.

Gradient descent then moves every weight a little against its own gradient. You will not code backpropagation in this course. A library does it. What matters is the loop: forward, loss, backward, adjust. Which step is the new idea for you?

title.text:
One epoch is one pass over the
training set, made of many batches

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsj_epoch_11.90x4.25_f56c37fc.png
objects.alt: One epoch is one pass over the training set, made of many batches

objects.text: MLPClassifier uses batches of up to 200 records by default (check your version).

slides.notes:
Two more training words. A batch is the group of records the network looks at before it adjusts its weights once. An epoch is one full pass over the training set. In our loans, the training set has 6,000 records. With batches of up to 200, that is 30 batches, so one epoch makes 30 adjustments of the weights.

Training runs for many epochs, and in scikit-learn the setting max_iter limits them. Why not adjust the weights only once per epoch, after all the records?

title.text:
Overfitting again: after epoch 50 the training
loss keeps falling and the test loss rises

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsj_lines_11.90x4.25_400598a5.png
objects.alt: Overfitting again: after epoch 50 the training loss keeps falling and the test loss rises

objects.text: A 12-64-64-1 network on only 300 training loans. Epochs run along the bottom.

slides.notes:
This picture shows overfitting again. I trained a larger network, with 5,057 parameters, on only 300 loans, and measured the loss on those 300 and on 2,000 loans it never saw. The black line, the training loss, keeps falling toward zero. The red line, the test loss, reaches its lowest value around epoch 50, then climbs.

The network is memorising the 300 loans. At the end its AUC on the training loans is 1.00, and on the test loans 0.63. A training score alone would have fooled us. Which score would you quote to a manager?

title.text: Four ways to fight overfitting in a network

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_gear_0.70.png

objects.text: Use fewer neurons or fewer layers: a smaller network has less room to memorise.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_shield_0.70.png

objects.text: Regularisation: MLPClassifier has an alpha setting that penalises large weights.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_clock_0.70.png

objects.text: Early stopping: stop training when the validation loss stops improving (early_stopping=True).

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_folder_0.70.png

objects.text: More training records: the most reliable cure when you can get them. Always judge on the test set.

slides.notes:
There are four standard ways to fight overfitting in a network. Use fewer neurons or fewer layers, so there is less room to memorise. Use regularisation: in scikit-learn the alpha setting of MLPClassifier penalises large weights. Use early stopping, which stops training when the validation loss stops improving, and which you switch on with early stopping equals true.

And get more training records, which is the most reliable cure. Whatever you do, judge on the test set and never on the training score. Which of these would you try first on the loans?

title.text:
Network or forest on a table?
Make the network earn its place

objects.text: Neural network (MLP)

runs.text: Many settings. Trains with Adam by default, a smarter gradient descent.
Hard to explain to a manager.

objects.text: Random forest

runs.text: Works on raw numbers, no scaling.

objects.text: On a table, start simple. Keep the network only if it wins by enough to matter.

slides.notes:
Now the practical question. For a table of numbers like the loans, which do you use?

A neural network needs imputing and scaling, has many settings, and is hard to explain to a manager. In scikit-learn the MLPClassifier trains with a variant of gradient descent called Adam by default: the same idea with smarter step sizes. A random forest works on raw numbers, has few settings with strong defaults, and shows which variables mattered.

My understanding of published comparisons is that on tables, tree-based models often match or beat neural networks. That is a general finding, so test it on your own data. The rule is simple: start with the simpler model, and make the network earn its place. What would count as winning by enough to matter?

title.text:
On the loans table a numpy network does no better

slides.notes:
Here is what I measured in numpy on the same eight thousand loans and the same two thousand test loans as Sessions 14 to 17. Logistic regression, which is a network with no hidden layer, reaches a test AUC of 0.758 with 13 parameters. My numpy network with sixteen and eight hidden neurons reaches 0.742 with 353 parameters.

So on this table the extra parameters buy nothing. Your scikit-learn runs in the lab will land near these numbers. And the column collection calls would push the AUC above 0.99, because it only exists after a loan goes bad. That is data leakage again. What would you recommend to the credit team?

title.text:
Transfer learning reuses a pretrained
model and trains only a new last layer

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsj_transfer_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Transfer learning reuses a pretrained model and trains only a new last layer

objects.text: Pretrained model: trained by someone else. Inference: using a trained model to predict.

slides.notes:
Some tasks, like recognising objects in photos, need networks with millions of parameters and huge training sets. You will not train those. You reuse a pretrained model, which someone else trained on a large collection of images. The early layers have learned general things, like edges, colours and textures.

The middle layers have learned shapes. In transfer learning we freeze those layers and replace the last layer with a new one, which we train on our own photos. That needs only a small number of labelled photos. And using a trained model to predict, without training it, is called inference.

What photos could you label in your own work?

title.text:
Four terms for using a network
somebody else trained

rows.text: A network already trained on a large dataset by someone else.
An image classifier published on the Hugging Face Hub
Using a trained model to predict. No training happens.
Reuse the early layers and train a new last layer on your own data.
A few hundred labelled photos of your own crops (illustrative)
Also adjust some of the pretrained weights, with a small learning rate.
Needs more data and more care

objects.text: Before you use a pretrained model at work, read its model page: the licence, the training data and the download size.

slides.notes:
Four terms to keep apart. A pretrained model is a network someone else trained on a large dataset. Inference means using a trained model to predict, with no training. Transfer learning means reusing the early layers and training a new last layer on your own data. Fine-tuning goes further and also adjusts some of the pretrained weights, with a small learning rate, so it needs more data and more care.

Before you use a pretrained model at work, read its model page, and check the licence, the training data and the download size. Which of the four would a small team with a few hundred photos use?

When deep learning is worth it:
match the tool to the kind of data

slides.notes:
So when is deep learning worth it?

For a table of numbers, like loans, orders or clinic visits, start with logistic regression, a random forest or gradient boosting, because you have few records per variable and you must explain the result. For images, use a pretrained network with transfer learning. For text and speech, use a pretrained language or speech model, which we meet in the next sessions.

Only for very large data with a hard pattern do you train a deep network yourself, and that needs lots of data and computing power, often a GPU. Which kind of data do you work with most?

title.text:
Read the recipe before the lab: a
network in a scikit-learn Pipeline

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: make_pipeline chains the imputer, the scaler and the network in order.
max_iter=500 limits the epochs. random_state=42 makes the run repeatable.
predict_proba gives the chance of default. roc_auc_score scores it on the test set.
You run this in the lab, and the AUC appears in your notebook.

slides.notes:
Read this recipe before the lab. Make pipeline chains three steps: the imputer fills blank incomes with the median, the scaler standardises each variable, and the MLPClassifier is the network. Hidden layer sizes sixteen and eight gives the two hidden layers from our picture. Max iter limits the number of epochs, and random state makes the run repeatable.

Predict proba gives the chance of default for each test loan, and roc auc score turns those chances into the AUC. Because the imputer sits inside the pipeline, the median comes from the training rows only. Sessions 14 to 17 computed it on all loans before the split, on purpose, to keep things simple.

No output is shown here, because you will produce it yourself. Why must the scaler sit inside the pipeline?

objects.text: Sketch of the screen. The real page may look different. Free, in the browser, no account.

slides.notes:
TensorFlow Playground is a free page in your browser where you can build a small network and watch it learn. This is a sketch of the screen, and the real page may look a little different. On the left you choose the data, such as circles or a spiral, and set the noise.

Then you choose the input features. In the middle you add hidden layers and neurons with the plus and minus buttons. On the right you see the dots coloured by the network, and the training loss and test loss. The bar at the top holds the learning rate and the activation function.

Press play, and watch. What do you expect a network with no hidden layer to do with the circle?

title.text:
Four Playground challenges: change
one thing and write down what you see

rows.text: Start with no hidden layer. Then add one hidden layer with 4 neurons.
Can it separate the circle each time? How long does it take?
Add a second hidden layer and more neurons.
The test loss before and after. Which size is enough?
Raise the noise, use few training points, train for a long time.
When do the training loss and the test loss separate?
Try a very small and a very large learning rate. Try ReLU and tanh (a bend that gives values from -1 to 1).
Which settings fail, which are slow, which are fast?

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: Training stopped before the loss settled.
Raise max_iter, or accept it if the AUC is stable.
Put SimpleImputer first in the Pipeline.
collection_calls is in X. It leaks the answer.
The loop weight becomes huge or nan
The learning rate is too big.
Use 0.05 and look at each step.
Your AUC differs from the slides
Random starting weights, or a different split.
Up to about 0.03 is expected. Above 0.05 means a different split or variable list.

slides.notes:
Five messages you may meet. A ConvergenceWarning about maximum iterations means training stopped before the loss settled, so raise max iter, or accept it if the AUC is stable. A ValueError about NaN means blank incomes reached the network, so put the imputer first. An AUC above 0.99 means collection calls is in your variables, and it leaks the answer.

A weight that becomes huge or nan means the learning rate is too big. And a small difference from my numbers is normal. Read the message first. It usually tells you the answer.

title.text:
Exit check: three questions, then
compare with the short answers

rows.text: What does one artificial neuron compute?
A weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function such as sigmoid or ReLU.
In gradient descent, what does the learning rate control, and what happens if it is too big?
The size of each step. Too big and the weight overshoots, bounces or blows up.
A network scores 1.00 AUC on the training loans and 0.65 on the test loans. What is wrong and what do you try?
Overfitting. Try a smaller network, regularisation, early stopping or more records, and quote the test score.
